chapter_title: Polymorphism and Virtual Functions: Dynamic Behavior

screens.title: Polymorphism & Virtual Functions
screens.subtitle: How C++ objects take many forms at runtime to enable flexible, extensible code

narration.text: Polymorphism gives objects the ability to behave differently depending on their real type at runtime. In C++ this dynamic behavior is driven by virtual functions and base-class pointers or references. You will learn why polymorphism makes collections, plugins, and interfaces much simpler to build, how the language selects the right function at runtime, and important pitfalls such as object slicing and destructor safety. We will use familiar examples — an Animal family of classes and a Shape hierarchy — to see non-virtual behavior, then convert functions to virtual to restore the intended behavior. You will also learn the difference between ordinary virtual functions, pure virtual functions that define an interface, and abstract classes that cannot be instantiated. Practical language features from C++11, like override and final, keep your inheritance hierarchies safer and clearer. Finally, we’ll underline a safety rule: when using polymorphism, make base destructors virtual so derived resources are cleaned up correctly. By the end of this lesson you’ll be able to explain runtime dispatch, avoid slicing, create abstract interfaces, and use override/final to prevent subtle bugs.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Virtual functions + base pointers/references enable runtime selection of the correct derived behavior; avoid slicing by using pointers/references and make base destructors virtual.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this lesson

narration.text: These objectives break the chapter into practical skills you can measure. First, you will be able to define polymorphism in C++ and explain why creating code that operates on base interfaces simplifies extension. Second, you will understand virtual functions and how runtime dispatch selects the correct derived method when you call through a base pointer or reference, unlike static calls resolved at compile time. Third, you will explain the slicing problem: what happens when a derived object is assigned to a base object by value, why derived data is lost, and why pointers or references prevent that loss. Fourth, you will differentiate virtual functions from pure virtual functions and recognize when to design an abstract class as a contract for derived types. Each objective includes a short mnemonic to make the skill easier to recall and a verified competency milestone you can use to self-check your understanding.

screens.title: What is Polymorphism?
screens.subtitle: Treating different derived objects through a common base interface

narration.text: Polymorphism means 'many forms' and in C++ it refers to the ability of different classes to respond differently to the same function call when used through a base class pointer or reference. This is not a compile-time trick; it is a runtime behavior where the program selects the most-derived implementation available. Conceptually, polymorphism lets you program to an interface: you write code that calls a common method on the base type and you let each concrete type provide its own implementation. A practical example is a graphics engine that stores Shape pointers: each derived shape implements calculateArea differently, and the engine simply iterates shapes and asks for areas without needing type checks. A common misconception is that polymorphism happens automatically for all functions. In C++, it only happens when functions are declared virtual and you invoke them through a pointer or reference to the base. If you call a non-virtual method directly on a derived object, the derived implementation runs, but calls through base types will use the base implementation. Another pitfall is storing polymorphic objects by value — this causes slicing and defeats polymorphism. Key takeaway: design your public base methods that form the interface as virtual when you expect derived classes to override them, and use pointers or references so the entire derived object is referenced. How might this change how you organize collections of related objects in your program?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Polymorphism means invoking a method on a base type and having the runtime choose the derived override based on actual object type.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › What is Polymorphism?
Core Concept

Polymorphism

Treat different derived objects uniformly through a common base interface and rely on runtime dispatch to call the correct behavior.

Key idea
Polymorphism requires virtual functions and calls via base pointers or references to select the most-derived implementation at runtime.
Misconception
Declaring a function in a derived class does not make base-class calls polymorphic; you must declare the base function virtual and invoke through a pointer or reference.
Why it matters
It eliminates type-based conditionals, centralizes behavior, and makes code easier to extend when new derived types are added.
Key Takeaway

Declare base methods virtual when you expect derived classes to override them and always call through pointers or references to enable runtime selection.

Concrete example
Shapes collection

Store Shape* pointers to Circle and Rectangle in a vector and call calculateArea on each. Each derived type computes area using its own formula without type checks.

Analogy

Think of a remote control labeled 'Play' that calls different device implementations based on the connected device: same button, different behavior.

Check your understanding

If a function is virtual but you store objects by value in a container, will polymorphism fire? No — slicing prevents it. Use pointers or references instead.

screens.title: How virtual functions enable dynamic dispatch
screens.subtitle: The runtime chooses the correct override when called through a base pointer/reference

narration.text: Dynamic dispatch is the mechanism by which C++ picks the right function implementation at runtime. The process starts with a function marked virtual in the base class. When a derived class overrides that function, the compiler ensures a runtime dispatch table, often called a vtable, exists so calls through a base pointer or reference look up the appropriate function at runtime. The key steps: declare the base method virtual; override it in derived types; store or pass objects via base pointers or references; call the method through that base pointer/reference and allow the runtime to dispatch to the derived override. A common error is to call the virtual method on a base object copy — because that copy is a base object, the dispatch chooses the base implementation. As a concrete example, create Animal* pointing to Dog and call makeSound: Dog's version runs. Remember that non-virtual functions are resolved at compile time, so the base signature determines which body is called when invoking on a base-typed reference or pointer. Takeaway: virtual enables late binding; pointer/reference invocation completes it. How will you structure your class interfaces to accept derived types without knowing them in advance?

keyIdea.title: Process
keyIdea.text: Virtual keyword + base pointer/reference + runtime vtable lookup = dynamic dispatch of the most-derived override.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Dynamic Dispatch
Process Flow

How virtual functions enable dispatch

Follow these steps to make calls resolve at runtime.

1. Declare virtual
Give the base method the virtual keyword to signal runtime override.
2. Override in derived
Implement the method in each derived class using matching signature.
3. Use base pointers/refs
Store or pass objects via Base* or Base& so runtime type is preserved.
4. Call and dispatch
Call through base pointer/reference and runtime chooses the derived override.
Concrete example

Animal* pet = new Dog("Buddy"); pet->makeSound(); results in Dog's makeSound running because the call goes through a base pointer.

Common mistake

Calling through a base object copy uses the base type's method and defeats polymorphism – that is object slicing.

Key Takeaway

Make the base method virtual and invoke it via pointer or reference to get dynamic behavior at runtime.

screens.title: Animal / Dog / Cat — Virtual makeSound walkthrough
screens.subtitle: See a working polymorphic example and how override is used

narration.text: Let's walk through a concise example that shows polymorphism in action. The base class Animal declares virtual void makeSound() const and a virtual destructor. Derived classes Dog and Cat override makeSound and mark it with override to ensure the signatures match the base declaration. In main, we allocate Dog and Cat objects on the heap and hold them with Animal* pointers. Calling makeSound via those pointers triggers Dog's and Cat's implementations respectively. We also show a vector of Animal* to represent a polymorphic collection that can store different derived instances. Finally, cleanup deletes each pointer and triggers derived destructors because the base destructor is virtual. A misconception to avoid: marking the destructor virtual is not optional when you intend polymorphic deletion — skipping it can silently skip derived cleanup and leak resources. This code illustrates both correct use of virtual functions and correct destructor practice. Animal / Dog / Cat — Virtual makeSound walkthrough means mark functions virtual in the base, use override in derived classes, hold objects via base pointers, and delete through base pointers with a virtual destructor.. In practical terms, see a working polymorphic example and how override is used. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Code example
keyIdea.text: Mark functions virtual in the base, use override in derived classes, hold objects via base pointers, and delete through base pointers with a virtual destructor.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Animal Example
Example Code

Polymorphic Animal classes

This snippet demonstrates virtual methods, override, and virtual destructor semantics.

#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

class Animal {
public:
  std::string name;
  Animal(const std::string& n) : name(n) {}
  virtual void makeSound() const {
    std::cout << name << " makes a generic animal sound." << std::endl;
  }
  virtual ~Animal() {
    std::cout << "Animal destructor called for " << name << std::endl;
  }
};

class Dog : public Animal {
public:
  Dog(const std::string& n) : Animal(n) {}
  void makeSound() const override {
    std::cout << name << " barks: Woof! Woof!" << std::endl;
  }
  ~Dog() override { std::cout << "Dog destructor called for " << name << std::endl; }
};

// ... similar Cat class ...

int main() {
  Animal* myDog = new Dog("Buddy");
  myDog->makeSound(); // Calls Dog's makeSound()
  delete myDog; // Calls Dog destructor then Animal destructor
  return 0;
}
Why override matters
override guarantees the derived signature matches a virtual base method; misspelling causes a compile error instead of a subtle bug.
Destructor safety
A virtual base destructor ensures derived destructors run when deleting via base pointers.
Explanation & example

Holding objects via Animal* preserves the derived identity. Calls to makeSound dispatch dynamically because the method is virtual. When deleting, the virtual destructor causes derived cleanup to run first.

Common misconception
Some assume override is optional; without it, a signature mismatch silently creates a new method rather than overriding and can break polymorphism.
Key Takeaway

Use virtual in base, override in derived, and always make the base destructor virtual if objects will be deleted via base pointers.

screens.title: Slicing: value semantics vs pointer/reference semantics
screens.subtitle: Why assigning a derived object to a base object by value removes derived parts

narration.text: The slicing problem happens when you copy a derived object into a base object by value. In that copy operation the derived-specific data and behavior are lost, leaving a pure base object. That means future calls on that object will use base implementations rather than derived overrides. For example, creating Dog buddy("Buddy"); Animal genericAnimal = buddy; slices off Dog parts and genericAnimal. makeSound() will call the base version. The correct approach when you need polymorphic behavior is to use pointers or references: Animal* p = &buddy; or Animal& r = buddy; both preserve the actual object and allow virtual calls to select Dog's implementation. Another concern is container storage: prefer std::vector<Animal*> or smart pointers like std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Animal>> to store polymorphic objects. A misconception is that slicing affects only data members; it also affects virtual behavior because the resulting object is a base instance. Key takeaway: avoid value storage for polymorphic objects and use pointers or references to preserve dynamic type. Slicing: value semantics vs pointer/reference semantics means assigning derived objects to base objects by value copies only the base subobject and strips away derived data and behavior; use pointers/references instead.. In practical terms, why assigning a derived object to a base object by value removes derived parts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Slicing
keyIdea.text: Assigning derived objects to base objects by value copies only the base subobject and strips away derived data and behavior; use pointers/references instead.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Slicing
Comparison

Value assignment vs pointer/reference

Compare the behaviors and choose the right storage for polymorphic objects.

Value assignment (slicing)

Derived object copied into base object loses derived fields and methods; virtual dispatch no longer reaches derived overrides because the object is now a base instance.

Pointer/reference

Pointing or referencing preserves the full derived object, so virtual calls still dispatch to the derived implementation.

Key Takeaway

Never store polymorphic objects by value if you expect derived behavior; use pointers, references, or smart pointers in containers.

Concrete code scenario

Dog buddy("Buddy"); Animal genericAnimal = buddy; // slicing: genericAnimal behaves like Animal, not Dog.

Recommended container

Use std::vector<Animal*> or std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Animal>> so each element keeps its derived identity and virtual calls work as expected.

Misconception

Some expect virtual to override slicing; it cannot. Slicing happens at the object level, before any virtual dispatch can occur.

screens.title: Pure virtual functions & Abstract classes
screens.subtitle: Designing base types as contracts that derived types must implement

narration.text: A pure virtual function is a virtual function declared with = 0 in the base class, indicating the base provides no implementation and that derived classes must implement it. A class containing at least one pure virtual function becomes abstract and cannot be instantiated directly. Use abstract classes to define interfaces: they spell out required behavior without tying you to a specific implementation. For example, Shape can declare virtual double calculateArea() const = 0; and each derived class such as Circle and Rectangle must provide calculateArea. Abstract classes are especially useful when you want to ensure a consistent A P I across many types and to prevent misuse by instantiation of an incomplete base. A common confusion is thinking abstract = interface; while similar, an abstract class can still include implemented helpers, constructors, or non-virtual members to share code among derived classes. Key takeaway: use pure virtual functions when you need a compile-time contract and enforce implementation in derived classes. Pure virtual functions & Abstract classes means pure virtual functions define required behavior and make the base class abstract, preventing direct instantiation and enforcing implementation in derived types.. In practical terms, designing base types as contracts that derived types must implement. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Abstract base
keyIdea.text: Pure virtual functions define required behavior and make the base class abstract, preventing direct instantiation and enforcing implementation in derived types.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Pure Virtual & Abstract
Definition

Pure virtual functions

Declare a function with = 0 to force derived classes to implement it and to make the base class abstract.

Example

virtual double calculateArea() const = 0; in Shape ensures every concrete shape provides an area computation.

Behavior

Attempting to instantiate Shape directly will cause a compile error because it's abstract.

Key Takeaway

Use pure virtual functions to define interfaces and make incomplete base classes abstract so only complete derived types can be instantiated.

Starter code (concept)
class Shape {
public:
  virtual double calculateArea() const = 0;
  virtual ~Shape() {}
};

class Circle : public Shape {
  double calculateArea() const override { /* ... */ }
};
Misconception

An abstract class can still contain implemented methods or data; it's not an empty interface unless you make it so.

screens.title: Implementing Polymorphic Shapes — Starter code
screens.subtitle: Make Shape abstract, implement Circle and Rectangle, and use a vector of Shape*

narration.text: This hands-on task guides you through making Shape an abstract base class and using polymorphism to compute areas. First, declare calculateArea as a pure virtual function and keep a virtual destructor. Then implement calculateArea in Circle and Rectangle using the correct formulas. In main, create a std::vector<Shape*> and push dynamically allocated Circle and Rectangle instances into it. Iterate the vector, calling displayColor and calculateArea on each Shape* to see polymorphism in action. Finally, delete each element to run destructors and clear the vector. This activity reinforces several lessons: abstract base classes as contracts, storing polymorphic objects via pointers to avoid slicing, the need to delete dynamically allocated objects, and the role of virtual destructors to call derived cleanup. A typical learner mistake is to use std::vector<Shape> or to forget delete; both break polymorphism or leak memory. Prefer smart pointers in production, such as std::unique_ptr<Shape> inside the vector, to automate cleanup. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Hands-on Shapes

Starter Code

Modify the base class to be abstract, implement derived areas, and use a polymorphic container.

#include <iostream>
#include <cmath> // For M_PI
#include <vector>

class Shape {
protected:
  std::string color;
public:
  Shape(const std::string& c) : color(c) {}
  void displayColor() const { std::cout << "This shape is " << color << "." << std::endl; }
  virtual double calculateArea() const = 0; // pure virtual
  virtual ~Shape() { std::cout << "Shape destructor called for color: " << color << std::endl; }
};

// Circle and Rectangle implement calculateArea and override destructor
Run checklist
  1. Make calculateArea pure virtual.
  2. Implement Circle and Rectangle calculateArea.
  3. Create std::vector<Shape*> and add objects.
  4. Iterate, call methods, delete objects.
Pro tip
Prefer smart pointers like std::unique_ptr to manage ownership and avoid manual delete in real code.
Concrete expectation

When you iterate the vector and call calculateArea on each Shape*, each derived implementation will compute its area correctly. Deleting the pointers will call derived destructors first then the base destructor if it is virtual.

Key Takeaway

Make Shape abstract to force derived implementation, store polymorphic objects via pointers, and clean up properly to observe polymorphism.

screens.title: override and final (C++11)
screens.subtitle: Improve safety and express intent when overriding virtual functions

narration.text: C++11 added override and final to make inheritance safer and clearer. The override keyword on a derived method tells the compiler you intend to override a virtual function from the base. If the signatures do not match exactly, the compiler produces an error rather than silently creating a separate method. This prevents bugs where a small typo or mismatched const-ness causes your method not to override the base. The final specifier can be applied to either a virtual function or a class. When applied to a function, it prevents further derived classes from overriding that function. When applied to a class, it prevents any inheritance from that class. Use final to lock down behaviour in an A P I when further modification would be unsafe. A common misconception is that override changes runtime behaviour — it does not; it only instructs the compiler to enforce your intent. Both keywords help maintainers and compilers catch unintentional mistakes early. override and final (C++11) means use override to catch signature mismatches at compile-time and final to prevent further overriding when required by design.. In practical terms, improve safety and express intent when overriding virtual functions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: override & final
keyIdea.text: Use override to catch signature mismatches at compile-time and final to prevent further overriding when required by design.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › override & final
Language Feature

override and final

Annotate intent and let the compiler help you catch mistakes or lock behavior.

override

Place override after the derived method signature to ensure it matches a base virtual method; a mismatch becomes a compile-time error.

final

Use final on a virtual function to prevent further overrides, or on a class to prevent inheritance.

Key Takeaway

Annotate overridden functions with override and use final to fix an API surface when extension would be unsafe or confusing.

Example scenario

If you intend to override void draw() const but accidentally write void draw(), using override causes the compiler to complain about the missing const — saving a subtle runtime bug.

Misconception

override and final are compile-time safety tools. They do not change dynamic dispatch semantics but prevent programmer errors that could break those semantics.

screens.title: Virtual destructors — preventing resource leaks
screens.subtitle: Why base destructors must usually be virtual for polymorphic classes

narration.text: When you delete a derived object through a base class pointer, the base destructor must be virtual to ensure the derived destructor runs. If the base destructor is not virtual, only the base destructor executes and derived cleanup is skipped. This can cause resource leaks when derived classes manage memory, file handles, or other resources. The rule of thumb: if a class has any virtual functions or is intended to be used polymorphically, give it a virtual destructor. The code example demonstrates this: Animal declares virtual ~Animal(), and derived classes override it. Deleting Animal* p = new Dog("Buddy"); triggers Dog's destructor, then Animal's destructor, releasing derived resources safely. A common misconception is thinking virtual destructors are only needed when derived classes have explicit delete logic; even implicitly-managed resources can leak if destructors are skipped. Key takeaway: virtual destructors enable correct cleanup order in polymorphic hierarchies and protect you from subtle memory or resource errors. Virtual destructors — preventing resource leaks means make the base destructor virtual when the class is used polymorphically so derived destructors run during deletion through base pointers.. In practical terms, why base destructors must usually be virtual for polymorphic classes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Virtual destructor
keyIdea.text: Make the base destructor virtual when the class is used polymorphically so derived destructors run during deletion through base pointers.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Virtual Destructors
Critical Safety

Virtual destructors

Ensure derived destructors are called when deleting through a base pointer to avoid leaking resources.

What can go wrong

If the base destructor is non-virtual, deleting a derived object via a base pointer calls only the base destructor, skipping derived cleanup.

Rule of thumb

If a class has virtual functions or is used polymorphically, make its destructor virtual.

Key Takeaway

Virtual destructor ensures correct destruction order: derived destructor first, then base destructor, preventing leaks.

Concrete example

Animal* p = new Dog("Buddy"); delete p; // Derived destructor runs first only if ~Animal() is virtual.

Common misconception

Virtual destructors are not needed only for explicit new/delete; they are essential whenever polymorphic deletion may occur, even indirectly through containers of pointers.

screens.title: Common mistakes and how to avoid them
screens.subtitle: Slicing, missing virtual, forgetting override, and non-virtual destructors

narration.text: Polymorphism is powerful, but there are recurring mistakes students make when implementing it. First, slicing — storing polymorphic objects by value — prevents virtual calls and loses derived data. Fix: use pointers or references or smart pointers in containers. Second, forgetting to declare base methods virtual means calls through base pointers never dispatch to derived overrides. Fix: mark intended override points virtual in the base. Third, omitting override in derived methods allows silent mismatches where a typo changes the signature and produces a new method rather than overriding. Fix: annotate derived overrides with override so the compiler catches mismatches. Fourth, non-virtual base destructors skip derived cleanup on deletion via base pointers; always make destructors virtual in polymorphic bases. Finally, overusing inheritance without a clear interface or using public data breaks encapsulation — favor composition when a true is-a relationship doesn't exist. The takeaway is to design carefully, annotate intent, and prefer smart pointers to manage lifetime safely. Common mistakes and how to avoid them means use pointers or smart pointers, declare virtual base methods and destructors, use override to catch signature errors, and prefer clear interfaces.. In practical terms, slicing, missing virtual, forgetting override, and non-virtual destructors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Avoid pitfalls
keyIdea.text: Use pointers or smart pointers, declare virtual base methods and destructors, use override to catch signature errors, and prefer clear interfaces.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Common Mistakes
Comparison

Common mistakes and fixes

Slicing

Cause: storing derived by value. Fix: use pointers/references or smart pointers.

Missing virtual

Cause: base method is not virtual. Fix: declare base method virtual to enable dynamic dispatch.

No override

Cause: signature mismatch silently creates new method. Fix: use override to force compile-time checks.

Non-virtual destructor

Cause: only base destructor runs on delete. Fix: make base destructor virtual for polymorphic classes.

Pro tip

Favor std::unique_ptr<Base> in containers to prevent leaks and avoid manual delete while preserving polymorphism.

screens.title: Designing with polymorphism: interfaces vs implementations
screens.subtitle: Use abstract bases for interface contracts and concrete classes for implementations

narration.text: When designing systems, separate the interface (what operations are required) from the implementation (how those operations are performed). Abstract base classes with pure virtual functions express the interface and enforce the contract. Concrete derived classes implement the required behavior. This separation lets client code depend only on the abstract interface, minimizing coupling and making it simple to add new types later. For instance, a rendering system can depend on Drawable with a pure virtual draw method; new object types implement draw without changing existing rendering code. Another advantage is testability: mock implementations of abstract interfaces are easy to create for unit tests. A misconception is that inheritance should be used for code reuse only; prefer composition when sharing implementation is the goal. Use inheritance primarily when the relationship is truly is-a and when the base defines required behavior. Key takeaway: model interfaces as abstract bases and keep behavior-specific details inside concrete types. Designing with polymorphism: interfaces vs implementations means favor abstract base classes to define required behavior, and let concrete classes implement details so you can change implementations without changing clients.. In practical terms, use abstract bases for interface contracts and concrete classes for implementations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Design with Polymorphism
Architecture

Interfaces vs Implementations

Define stable interfaces with abstract bases and keep implementation details in derived classes for flexibility and testability.

Client code

Depends on the abstract base type and calls virtual methods; it should not depend on concrete derived types.

Concrete implementers

Implement required virtual functions and encapsulate implementation details; new implementations can be added without changing clients.

Key Takeaway

Design APIs around abstract bases and keep concrete details isolated so your system remains extensible and testable.

Analogy

Think of an electrical socket as the interface and different appliance plugs as implementations; new appliances work without changing the socket.

Misuse warning

Do not use inheritance purely for code reuse. Prefer composition if shared behavior can be factored into member objects rather than imposing an is-a relationship.

screens.subtitle: Safe ownership of polymorphic objects with unique_ptr and shared_ptr

narration.text: When working with polymorphic collections prefer smart pointers to manual new/delete to avoid leaks and improve exception safety. std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Base>> transfers ownership of each derived object into the container and automatically calls the correct derived destructor when the unique pointer is destroyed. std::shared_ptr<Base> provides shared ownership semantics when many parts of code must hold a reference. The stored pointer type still preserves the dynamic type, so virtual functions dispatch normally. Key steps: dynamically allocate derived objects, wrap them in a smart pointer to Base, and add to the container. This approach avoids slicing, ensures cleanup, and aligns with RAII. A common misconception is that smart pointers change polymorphic behavior — they do not; they only manage lifetime. Use smart pointers as a best practice for real-world code to prevent manual memory management errors while preserving polymorphism. Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Smart Pointers
Practical Tip

Smart pointers & polymorphism

Use smart pointers in containers to manage lifetime while preserving dynamic dispatch.

Recommended pattern
std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Shape>> shapes;
shapes.push_back(std::make_unique<Circle>("Red", 5.0));
shapes.push_back(std::make_unique<Rectangle>("Blue", 4.0, 6.0));
for (const auto &s : shapes) {
  s->displayColor();
  std::cout << "Area: " << s->calculateArea() << std::endl;
}
Key Takeaway

Smart pointers preserve polymorphism and automate destruction; prefer them over raw pointers in modern C++ containers.

Why smart pointers?

They prevent memory leaks, are exception-safe, and ensure the correct derived destructor runs because the stored type retains polymorphic identity.

Misconception

Smart pointers don't change how virtual dispatch works; they only manage lifetime. Polymorphism still requires virtual functions and base pointers or references.

narration.text: Here are the core concepts to retain. First, polymorphism allows different concrete types to respond to the same message at runtime, enabling flexible and extensible code. Second, virtual functions enable dynamic dispatch: declare the base function virtual and call it through a base pointer or reference so the runtime chooses the derived override. Third, avoid slicing by never storing polymorphic objects by value — use pointers, references, or smart pointers in containers. Use override to ensure your derived methods truly match base signatures and final to lock behavior when needed. Finally, always make base destructors virtual if the class is polymorphic so derived destructors run and resources are cleaned up. These compact ideas will guide safe, maintainable use of polymorphism in C++.
